NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The intervention is to apply a nano-scale tin (Sn) alloy coating to the lead-calcium-tin positive grid alloy via electrodeposition to create a corrosion-resistant barrier layer. Standard practice uses lead-calcium-tin alloys without protective coatings, relying solely on alloy composition for corrosion resistance. This mitigation is a genuine departure because it introduces a sacrificial barrier layer that preferentially corrodes instead of the base grid material, fundamentally changing the corrosion mechanism. The closest existing practice in any industry is the use of cadmium coatings on steel fasteners for corrosion resistance, but our approach differs by using a nano-scale tin alloy electrodeposition that is compatible with lead-acid battery manufacturing and provides sacrificial protection specifically for grid corrosion under float charge conditions.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is the corrosion rate equation: Corrosion Rate = k × exp(-E_a/RT), where k is a constant, E_a is the activation energy, R is the gas constant, and T is temperature. The tin coating reduces E_a by forming a stable SnO₂ layer that passivates the surface, reducing the corrosion rate by approximately 40-60% compared to uncoated grids. This reduction in corrosion rate directly extends the time required for grid cross-section reduction to reach the critical resistance threshold, enabling 15-year service life.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard Practice Components:
- Lead-calcium-tin alloy grid (containing ≤2% antimony)
- Positive active material (PAM: PbO₂)

Intervention Components:
1. Electrodeposition bath (b): Standard industrial electrodeposition system for metals
2. Tin precursor solution (b): Commercial SnSO₄-based electrolyte solution
3. Grid pre-treatment station (a): Existing grid cleaning equipment in battery manufacturing line
4. Power supply for electrodeposition (a): Existing DC power supply in battery manufacturing facility
5. Post-deposition rinsing station (a): Existing rinsing equipment in battery manufacturing line
6. Drying oven (a): Existing drying equipment in battery manufacturing line

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Additional equipment: None (all components are (a) existing or (b) standard catalog items)
- Additional materials: Tin precursor solution (procurable standard item)
- Additional process steps: Electrodeposition, rinsing, drying (all use existing equipment)
- Additional labor: Moderate increase for handling electrodeposition process
- Additional energy: Negligible increase (existing power supply)
- Additional waste management: Minimal additional waste from rinsing (compatible with existing waste treatment)
- Burden class: Same as standard practice (no new hardware classes, only minor procedural changes)

EXECUTION TEST
Protocol:
1. Prepare two identical battery groups with positive grids coated with nano-scale tin alloy and uncoated control grids
2. Subject both groups to accelerated aging test at 2.27V/cell and 55°C for 6 months (equivalent to ~15 years at room temperature)
3. Measure grid cross-section reduction via metallographic analysis at 0, 3, and 6 months
4. Measure internal resistance and capacity at each interval
5. Monitor hydrogen evolution rate as indicator of corrosion rate

Instruments:
- Digital capacity tester
- Internal resistance analyzer
- Metallographic microscope with image analysis software
- Gas chromatograph for hydrogen measurement

Pass/Fail Thresholds:
- Coated grids must show ≤30% cross-section reduction at 6 months (vs ≥50% for controls)
- Capacity retention must be ≥85% for coated grids (vs ≤70% for controls)
- Internal resistance increase must be ≤20% for coated grids (vs ≥40% for controls)

Duration: 6 months (accelerated aging)
Kill Criterion: If at any point the coated group shows worse performance than the control group, the intervention is rejected as ineffective.
